title: Expanding the Apex Court: A Detailed Analysis of the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill 2026
excerpt: In a significant move to address mounting judicial backlog and strengthen the Indian judiciary, the Union Cabinet approved the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026, to raise the Court's strength from 34 to 38 judges.
content:
In a significant move to address the mounting judicial backlog and strengthen the Indian judiciary, the Union Cabinet approved the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill 2026 on May 6, 2026. The bill aims to increase the sanctioned strength of Supreme Court judges to meet the evolving legal needs of the country.

## The News at a Glance

>> The proposed amendment seeks to increase the total number of judges from the current 34 to 38, including the Chief Justice of India. The proposal therefore raises the strength from 33 judges plus 1 Chief Justice to 37 judges plus 1 Chief Justice. This change requires a simple majority in both Houses of Parliament, followed by Presidential assent.

## Key Facts: Supreme Court Strength (2026)

- Proposed strength: 38 judges (37 Judges + 1 CJI)
- Current strength: 34 judges (33 Judges + 1 CJI), fixed in 2008
- Original strength in 1950: 8 judges (7 Judges + 1 CJI)
- Constitutional basis: Article 124(1)
- Amendment type: Simple majority in Parliament
- Expenditure: Charged to the Consolidated Fund of India

## Constitutional Framework: Article 124

The Constitution of India provides the roadmap for the structure and functioning of the Supreme Court.

- Article 124(1): Empowers Parliament to increase the number of judges by law. Initially, the Constitution provided for 8 judges but left room for expansion.
- Article 124(2): Deals with the appointment process through the President in consultation with judges, now effectively governed by the Collegium system.
- Article 124(3): Lays down qualifications. A judge must be a citizen of India and must have been a High Court judge for 5 years, or an advocate for 10 years, or be a distinguished jurist.

## Why is this Increase Necessary?

The judicial system has been facing several bottlenecks that necessitated this expansion.

- Massive pendency: As of late 2025, more than 92,000 cases were pending in the Supreme Court.
- Special Leave Petitions (SLPs): A significant portion of the Court's time, around 30 percent by the document's estimate, is consumed by admission hearings for SLPs under Article 136.
- Constitutional Benches: Because of the shortage of judges, 5-judge or 7-judge Constitution Benches were rarely able to sit regularly, delaying verdicts on critical constitutional matters.
- Vacancy management: The Court often operates with 3 to 6 vacancies, meaning actual working strength remains lower than sanctioned strength.

## Evolution of the SC Strength

The journey from 8 judges to 38 reflects the growing legal complexity of the Indian state.

- 1950: 8 judges
- 1956: 11 judges
- 1977: 18 judges
- 1986: 26 judges
- 2008: 34 judges
- 2026 (Proposed): 38 judges

## The Appointment Mechanism: The Collegium System

Judicial appointments in India are governed by the Collegium system, which evolved through the Three Judges Cases.

- First Judges Case (1981): Gave primacy to the executive.
- Second Judges Case (1993): Established the Collegium and gave primacy to the Chief Justice of India's opinion.
- Third Judges Case (1998): Expanded the Collegium to the Chief Justice of India plus the four senior-most judges.
- NJAC Judgment (2015): The Supreme Court struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission linked to the 99th Amendment in order to preserve judicial independence.

## Conclusion

The 2026 amendment is presented in the document as a proactive step toward judicial reform. By increasing bench strength, the judiciary may move closer to the goal of speedy justice, ensure more regular functioning of Constitution Benches, and better manage the continuing influx of new cases.

title: Supreme Court Rules Menstrual Hygiene Access a Constitutional Right
excerpt: The Supreme Court held that access to menstrual hygiene facilities in schools is a constitutional right, directing the central government to provide such facilities across all schools.
content:
The Supreme Court of India delivered a landmark ruling on April 7, 2026, holding that access to menstrual hygiene facilities in schools is a fundamental constitutional right.

The Court directed the central government to ensure adequate menstrual hygiene facilities in all government and government-aided schools, and further ordered that menstrual hygiene education be made mandatory for both male and female students.

The bench issued a 'continuous mandamus' order, requiring the government to file compliance reports every three months, ensuring the directive is implemented and not merely acknowledged on paper.

The judgment builds on the constitutional guarantee of the right to education under Article 21A and the broader right to dignity embedded in Article 21. Legal experts have called the ruling a significant step toward achieving substantive equality in educational access for girls across India.

title: Supreme Court: DA–DR Disparity Between Employees and Pensioners Violates Article 14
excerpt: The Supreme Court held that granting higher Dearness Allowance to serving employees than Dearness Relief to pensioners is arbitrary and unconstitutional under Article 14.
content:
In a significant ruling with wide-ranging implications for pension policy, the Supreme Court of India held on April 10, 2026, that the disparity between Dearness Allowance (DA) paid to serving employees and Dearness Relief (DR) paid to pensioners is unconstitutional.

The Court reasoned that both DA and DR share the identical objective of neutralising the impact of inflation on employees and retirees. Since the purpose is the same, differential treatment — paying serving employees a higher rate than pensioners — constitutes unreasonable classification that violates Article 14 (Right to Equality).

The ruling has significant fiscal implications for both central and state governments, which will now need to align DR rates with DA rates for their respective workforces. Pensioners' associations across the country welcomed the judgment as a long-overdue recognition of their rights.

Article 14 of the Constitution guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws within the territory of India — and the Court's ruling reaffirms that this equality extends to the treatment of retired government servants.

title: Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026 Receives Presidential Assent
excerpt: President Droupadi Murmu gave assent to the Transgender Persons Amendment Act, 2026, which replaces the right to self-identification with a medical board certification requirement.
content:
President Droupadi Murmu gave her assent on March 30, 2026 to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026, after it was passed by the Lok Sabha on March 24 and the Rajya Sabha on March 25.

The Amendment replaces the right to self-identified gender — which had been recognised by the Supreme Court in the landmark 2014 NALSA v. Union of India judgment — with a requirement that transgender persons obtain certification from a medical board.

Human rights organisations including Amnesty International and the International Commission of Jurists criticised the amendment as a major step backward. Critics argue that requiring medical board certification re-pathologises transgender identity and creates significant barriers to the legal recognition of gender.

Constitutional scholars have raised questions about whether the amendment adequately upholds Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21 — the equality, non-discrimination, freedom, and dignity provisions of the Constitution. Several petitions challenging the amendment are expected to be filed in the Supreme Court.

title: Special Parliament Session Called to Implement Women's Reservation Amendment
excerpt: The government has called a special three-day Parliament session (April 16–18) to introduce a Constitutional Amendment Bill for implementing the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam before the 2029 elections.
content:
The government called a special session of Parliament for April 16–18, 2026, to introduce a Constitutional Amendment Bill aimed at operationalising the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam — the Women's Reservation Law that was passed in 2023 as the 106th Constitutional Amendment.

The proposed amendment would increase the total number of Lok Sabha seats from 543 to 816, with 273 of the new seats reserved exclusively for women. The seats would be distributed across states in proportion to their population.

Both the ruling BJP and the opposition Congress have issued three-line whips for their members of Parliament, signalling the importance both parties attach to the vote. Congress, while supporting women's reservation in principle, has raised objections about the government's proposed delimitation methodology and the timeline.

The 106th Amendment (2023), while historic, had linked the commencement of reservations to the completion of a delimitation exercise and a census. The government now proposes to proceed with a fresh delimitation based on 2021 census projections, a move that critics — particularly from south Indian states — argue will reduce their seat count.

title: Constitution of India Released in Sindhi Language on Sindhi Bhasha Diwas
excerpt: Vice-President C. P. Radhakrishnan released an updated Constitution of India in the Sindhi language in both Devanagari and Persian scripts, as part of efforts to publish it in all Scheduled languages.
content:
On the occasion of Sindhi Bhasha Diwas on April 10, 2026, Vice-President C. P. Radhakrishnan formally released an updated edition of the Constitution of India in the Sindhi language.

Two editions were released — one in Devanagari script and one in Persian (Nastaliq) script — reflecting the dual-script tradition of the Sindhi language. The release makes the Constitution more accessible to Sindhi-speaking citizens across India.

Sindhi is one of the 22 languages listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution. The Eighth Schedule (Articles 343–351) deals with the official languages of India, and Article 351 directs the Union to promote the spread and development of the Hindi language while drawing on Sanskrit and scheduled languages including Sindhi.

The government has been working to publish the Constitution in all 22 Scheduled languages. The initiative is part of broader efforts to strengthen the connection between Indian citizens and their founding document, and to make constitutional literacy accessible across linguistic communities.
